title: Web platform patterns
summary: Operational web rules for semantic HTML, familiar UI patterns, pointer and viewport diversity, native browser behavior, and content-shaped layout. Each rule links the page for that subject.

rules.title: Semantic HTML
rules.intent: Choose elements for their meaning and built-in behavior, then add ARIA only when no native element expresses the widget
principles: Pick the element that matches the content's function: headings, lists, tables, buttons, and links, not a styled div
Expose page regions with header, nav, main, and footer so assistive tech can jump between landmarks
Keep heading levels in document order. A section needs a heading unless a more specific element already names it
Prefer a native control. Reach for ARIA when the widget has no HTML equivalent, such as a tab set
antiPatterns: A landmark on every small group, which turns the accessibility tree into noise
acceptance: Landmarks and headings are present and named
Interactive controls are native elements, or a documented ARIA pattern with keyboard behavior
limitations: These pages describe HTML semantics and accessible structure. They do not specify visual style

rules.title: Web conventions
rules.intent: Reuse patterns people already know how to operate, and change presentation across sizes without changing the meaning
principles: Keep global navigation the same on every page, and mark the current page
Adapt a known pattern to the viewport: a nav list, a table, or a set of cards can reflow, but the same items stay reachable
When a custom widget is required, follow a published ARIA pattern instead of inventing the keyboard model
antiPatterns: A small-screen layout that hides links with no visible way to reach them
acceptance: A person can predict where a control goes and what it does
Any custom widget names the APG pattern it follows
limitations: The UI patterns lesson covers responsive presentation of common components. It does not authorize replacing a product's own navigation system
A tested alternative can still replace a convention. These pages do not define the test

rules.title: Viewport and input diversity
rules.intent: Respond to viewport and input capabilities directly, instead of guessing touch from a narrow screen
principles: Choose breakpoints from the content, using min-width and min-height, not from a phone model list
Query pointer, any-pointer, and hover. A coarse pointer needs a larger target. Do not shrink targets just because a fine pointer exists
Do not hide an essential action behind hover. Pair hover styles with focus
Set the viewport meta to width=device-width and initial-scale=1 before relying on fluid layout
antiPatterns: Treating a narrow viewport as proof that the only input is a finger
acceptance: The layout is checked at narrow and wide widths, including a short wide window
Keyboard focus and a coarse pointer can both reach the primary actions
limitations: Media features report input capability. They do not replace a manual keyboard pass

rules.title: Native browser behavior
rules.intent: Leave back, text selection, autofill, and the person's choice of tab alone unless a specific control needs otherwise
principles: Keep pages eligible for the back/forward cache: avoid unload listeners and close connections on pagehide so Back restores the previous view
Let readable text use the user agent's selection behavior. Reserve user-select: none for a control where selection would fight the interaction
Hint fields with autocomplete, name, and type so the browser can offer saved data. Turn autofill off only for a one-off value such as a one-time code
Leave ordinary links in the current tab. People can already open a new tab. Use target=_blank only when leaving the page would discard their work, and do not spawn a new tab on every click
antiPatterns: autocomplete=off on a name, address, or password field
acceptance: Back returns to the previous view without a broken reload
Contact and address fields expose autocomplete tokens
In-app links do not force a new tab
limitations: MDN documents user-select. It does not forbid none. The restriction on body copy is operational guidance derived from the default
The links lesson explains target=_blank. It does not ban it

rules.title: Content-first layout
rules.intent: Settle the content order, the real string lengths, and the empty condition before choosing a layout
principles: Make the single-column content order sensible first. That order is what a narrow viewport gets
Check line length and type size against real copy, not a short placeholder
An empty panel states what is missing, whether the system is still working, and the next action. Do not show a false 'no records' message while data is still loading
antiPatterns: A blank container after a filter or a first visit, with no status and no way forward
acceptance: Fixtures use the longest realistic string and a true empty result
The narrow layout follows the document order
Empty, loading, and no-results are visibly different
limitations: Macro layouts and typography cover content order and reading comfort. Empty-state behavior comes from the NN/g article, which is research guidance, not a web platform specification
